entertainment.title: At ADE 2026, a Top Music Lawyer Talks AI, Independence & What the Biz Can Learn From Radiohead
entertainment.summary: Lawyer and music industry analyst Cliff Fluet laid out where power in the music industry is moving and who’s positioned to hold it.
entertainment.body:
Nineteen years ago this month, Radiohead released its seventh studio album, In Rainbows , and invited fans to pay whatever they wanted for it. Given that this announcement came amid rampant music piracy and the general collapse of the recorded music business, some took the move as proof that recorded music had lost its value, that the old model was broken and that artists would have to give their work away to survive.

But “the question was never really about price or value,” said Cliff Fluet , co-head of media and entertainment at U.K. law firm Lewis Silkin LLP, during a talk at last week’s Amsterdam Dance Event (ADE). “It was about who owns the relationship with the fan.”

Fluet used that moment in music history to center his wide-ranging talk at ADE 2026, the annual dance music industry gathering in Amsterdam that concluded this past weekend. Speaking to a packed room on Friday (Oct. 23), Fluet gave a talk titled “The State Of Things With Cliff Fluet” that spanned topics from AI to recent industry mega-deals and more. These topics all related to a central theme: Who currently holds power in the music industry, and how is that shifting?

The conversation happened as part of ADE Pro, the event’s programming track for those in the industry, which in total hosted 148 panels, 25 mixers and other sessions that brought the number of Pro programs to 188.

In the talk, Fluet argued that Radiohead wasn’t making a statement about what music was worth. Rather, he said, they were making a statement about engagement, independence and going direct — three principles that, nearly two decades later, still define where astute members of the music industry are focused.

A t a moment when the broader music industry is working to figure out direct-to-fan monetization, independent infrastructure and community building, electronic music is a sector that’s already been doing all of this for decades.

“I think electronic music shows the way, in so many ways, that the rest of the music industry isn’t spending enough time looking at,” Fluet said. “There’s so much more that the music industry could and should be learning.”

Fluet made the case that the superstar DJ model — an artist showing up with a USB, playing to thousands of people, collecting ticket revenue and building a devoted fanbase with minimal traditional industry infrastructure — is essentially the direct monetization blueprint the broader industry is now trying to replicate. “It’s a $15 billion scene, up 7%,” Fluet noted of the global dance industry’s 2025 valuation , “and it has always been about that direct monetization.”

entertainment.title: New Anthony Edwards Ad Takes Shots at Drake: ‘A Certain Bandwagon Fan Is Facing FOMO & Buried in Lawsuits’
entertainment.summary: This is the second time the NBA superstar has responded to a Kevin Durant & Drake Nike commercial from earlier this year.
entertainment.body:
The Anthony Edwards vs. Kevin Durant and Drake sneaker war doesn’t seem to be ending anytime soon.

In a new ad for the adidas AE 3, starring Hasan Minhaj as “The official Anthony Edwards insider,” the comedian and actor took a dig at he Toronto rapper in response to a Kevin Durant Nike commercial from a few months ago.

As he introduces himself, Minhaj makes a joke about your mom before taking a shot at LeBron James and Nike’s stock price, and finally focuses his attention at Drake. “Oh, and meanwhile, somewhere in Toronto, a certain bandwagon fan is facing FOMO and buried in lawsuits . Really sorry about that!” he says to the camera.

Back in June , Durant and Nike released an ad promoting a new purple colorway of the KD 19 where Drake and the sneakers are delivered in a wooden box to the Houston Rockets forward’s house. As Drake talks about the new kicks, he ends his sales pitch with a jab toward Anthony Edwards’s signature sneakers. “‘Hey Ant-Man, can you drop your purple shoes?’ Said four kids in Minnesota,” he jokes. “Like no one wants to see those, they want the KDs”

This is the second ad where Edwards responds to Nike’s commercial.

Earlier this month, in a PrizePicks ad , he parodied the aforementioned Nike ad and had a wooden box delivered to his friends to replace with a box of his sneakers. The box had “FRAGILE: RETURN TO TORONTO” stenciled on it, while someone was inside it trying to get out as they asked for Kevin. Once they realize who might be inside the box, his friend borrows a line from Kendrick Lamar . “Man, buddy ain’t nothin’,” he tells his partner. “You know he had to run to Atlanta to get the swag, anyway.”

After they switch the boxes up, they park in front of a crowd of people, walk out and say, “I heard only four people in Minnesota wanted these.”

We will have to wait and see if Ant-Man earned himself a couple of bars in Drake’s next song.

entertainment.title: Neil Young Hits Trump With $10M Lawsuit for Playing ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ at Rally — Again
entertainment.summary: “The song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for,” write Young’s attorneys in the copyright infringement complaint.
entertainment.body:
Years after Neil Young first sued Donald Trump for playing “Rockin’ in the Free World’ at political rallies, the rocker is once again taking the president’s team to court for using the 1989 hit without a license.

“’Rockin’ in the Free World’ is a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten,” reads Young’s lawsuit. “The lyrics paint vivid street-level portraits — a mother discarding her baby, addicts lost in despair, garbage piling in the shadows of prosperity — while the repeated chorus delivers a savage irony, celebrating freedom that clearly isn’t shared by all. In short, the song is the opposite of everything that Donald J. Trump stands for.”

Young claims he did not, and never would, grant Trump’s PAC a public performance license to use his song. The rocker says Trump should have known this was illegal because Young previously sued Trump’s campaign for the same thing during his 2020 presidential run. According to Young, Trump’s campaign quickly settled the 2020 lawsuit and promised that “it would never again use ‘Rockin’ in the Free World’ without a license and permission from Young.”

Now, since Trump is allegedly once again playing Young’s music without permission, the musician wants a legal injunction preventing further misuse. He’s also seeking hefty financial damages.

“Among other things, Young has suffered damage to his reputation and brand as a result of the implication that he supports Donald J. Trump in any way,” write Young’s lawyers.

The White House did not immediately return a request for comment on the lawsuit Monday.

Young is far from the only artist to challenge Trump for using their music at rallies. Scores of musicians have gone public with their distaste for the practice ever since Trump entered politics in 2016, and Young isn’t the only one who’s sued. In 2024, both The White Stripes and the estate of Isaac Hayes initiated lawsuits over Trump’s use of the songs “Seven Nation Army” and “Hold On, I’m Coming.” The White Stripes suit was quickly dropped , and the Hayes estate settled this year .

During Trump’s second term in office, his administration has also been beefing with pop stars like Sabrina Carpenter , Olivia Rodrigo and Ariana Grande over the use of their music in TikTok and Instagram posts. Many of these posts have been videos promoting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s deportation agenda under Trump.
